title: The sceptic's parables
hookLine: Prince Payasi argues against rebirth; Kumara Kassapa answers with stories

lines: HE ASKED THE DYING TO RETURN.
cards: Payasi is a ruler of the town of Setavya, and he has a firm view. There is no world after this one. No beings reborn.
No fruit of good or bad deeds. And he's not lazy about it. He's tested it.
He's asked dying friends who lived badly to come back and warn him, if there's anything after. None came. He's asked dying friends who lived well to come back and tell him.
None came. So he concludes: nothing. When a monk named Kumara Kassapa comes through, Payasi goes out to argue.

teach.h: A THIEF ON THE WAY TO EXECUTION.
teach.b: The Payasi Sutta, the twenty-third Long Discourse, is set after the Buddha's death, and it's almost all stories. To the first experiment, Kassapa answers with a thief.
A man is caught, and on the way to execution he says: let me go home first, just to say goodbye. Would the guards let him? No.
Then why expect someone in a hard rebirth to be allowed back to report? To the second, a man who has fallen into a pit of filth.

teach.h: A MAN PULLED FROM THE PIT.
teach.b: He's pulled out, scrubbed, perfumed, dressed in fine clothes. Would he want to go back down into the pit? No.
Then why expect someone in a happy world to come back here? Payasi tries harder experiments, and Kassapa answers with more stories.

teach.h: THE SHELL THAT WON'T SPEAK ALONE.
teach.b: A village hears a conch for the first time and asks the shell to speak again, but it only sounds when someone blows it with effort.
And at last, when Payasi says that even so, he can't give up a view he's known for, Kassapa tells one more.

teach.h: THE MAN WHO KEPT HIS HEMP.
teach.b: Two friends find a bundle of hemp. Later they find hemp thread, then cloth, then silver, then gold. One friend swaps up each time.
The other says: no, I've carried this hemp a long way, and it's well tied. And he walks home with the hemp.
Look at how Kassapa argues. He never mocks. He treats Payasi's doubt as a real question that deserves a real answer, and answers it with pictures anyone can weigh.
Whether you find the answers convincing is yours to decide. The sutta's respect for the question is plain.

how: Buddhist teachers often retell the parables of the Payasi Sutta, especially the hemp carrier, when talking about holding views, and many traditions treat honest doubt as a question to explore rather than a fault.

o: a scornful reply that ends a debate
a proof drawn from a dying friend
a simile, a picture used to explain

games.q: the sceptic's parables: tap the pairs.
p: the ruler who doubted any world beyond
the monk who answered with stories
not allowed home to say goodbye
kept his hemp instead of gold

s: Kassapa mocks Payasi for his doubts
he answers every argument with a story, treating the question seriously.
Payasi had actually tested his view by asking dying friends to return
none of them came back, so he concluded there was nothing after.
the Payasi Sutta takes place after the Buddha's death
Kumara Kassapa is teaching on his own.

games.q: you've carried a bundle of hemp a long way. your friend has traded his for gold and offers you the same. what do you do?
o: keep the hemp: it's well tied and you've carried it far.
games.why: in the story the second friend keeps his hemp, and Kassapa uses him as a picture of holding a view only because you're used to it.

practice: Bring to mind one doubt you hold, about a teaching, about yourself, about anything, and treat it the way Kassapa treated Payasi: as a fair question from someone worth talking to.
Breathe with it, then check gently: am I keeping this view because I've weighed it, or because I've carried it a long way? Either answer is fine.

wordCard.voice: Upama. In DN 23 Kumara Kassapa answers Payasi's doubts about rebirth with stories, never with scorn. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali upama: a simile, a comparison. Kassapa's whole method in DN 23.

carryVoice: Your line: a picture, not a put-down. Kassapa never mocks; he simply answers. Until tomorrow.
